**Video:** [Lec 06 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bdcvsSNAHIk)

### Learning goals
- See an image (or any data point) as a vector in the **range** of a random variable
- Separate **pixel values** from **probabilities**
- Model image + label as two RVs on one $\Omega$, with a joint $P_{X,Y}$
- State the course slogan: knowing the distribution means knowing the experiment

### Before this clicks
From Lectures 2–5: random variable $X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$, pushforward / distribution $P_{X}$, joints and conditionals. An $d$-dimensional RV is the same idea as $d$ scalar RVs on the same $\Omega$.

---

## 1. An image is a $D$-dimensional vector

Take an image of size $P\times Q$ pixels. In software it is a $P\times Q$ grid of numbers. Stack the rows into one long list and you get a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{PQ}$. Write

$$
D = PQ.
$$

So every image is a point in $\mathbb{R}^{D}$. The same story holds for any tabular feature vector: **a data point is a $D$-dimensional vector**.

---

## 2. That vector sits in the *range* of a random variable

In the probabilistic view:

$$
X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{D},
$$

and the image you store on disk is one value $x$ in the **range** of $X$ (one realization / observation).

Behind $X$ sit:

- an underlying random experiment with sample space $\Omega$,
- a probability measure $P$ on events,
- a pushforward distribution $P_{X}$ on (Borel) sets in $\mathbb{R}^{D}$.

> **Take-home line from class:** every data point is an element of the range space of a random variable.

What is $\Omega$ for “patients get X-rayed”? That is a **modeling choice** — you invent a coherent story for the experiment that produces the images (and later the labels).

---

## 3. Pixel values are *not* probabilities

A common confusion (asked in class): pixel intensities lie in $\{0,\ldots,255\}$ or $[0,1]$ after normalization — so are they probabilities?

**No.**

- A data point $x\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ is just a **real vector** (an outcome in the range).
- Probability lives on **events** (sets), via $P$ or the pushforward $P_{X}$.
- The distribution tells you the **likelihood of observing** (sets of) such vectors under the experiment — not that the vector entries themselves are probabilities.

Uniform-on-$[0,1/2]$ density equals $2$ everywhere on its support: that number is clearly **not** a probability (Lecture 9 will hammer this again for densities).

---

## 4. What the distribution is telling you

For continuous models you talk about subsets of the range, not single points. Roughly:

- subsets of images $\leftrightarrow$ inverse-image events in $\Omega$ $\leftrightarrow$ values of $P_{X}$.

Intuition used in class: $P_{X}$ quantifies how likely it is to **obtain that kind of image** under the experiment.

**Key slogan:**

> The distribution function completely specifies what we need to know about the underlying experiment (for the purposes of this course).

That is why the whole course is about **estimating distributions from samples**.

---

## 5. Labels = another random variable on the same $\Omega$

The X-ray story is not only “get an image”; a clinician also assigns a label (disease / no disease, or a bounding box, …).

Model:

$$
X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{D},\qquad Y:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{K}
$$

(or $Y$ discrete with a finite set of categories). Both sit on the **same** sample space. Calling $Y$ a “label” is nomenclature; mathematically it is just another RV.

| Task | Typical $Y$ |
|------|-------------|
| Binary disease | $Y\in\{0,1\}$ |
| Multi-class | $Y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ |
| Tumor box (center, height, width) | $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ |

Because both exist, there is a **joint** $P_{X,Y}$.

---

## 6. The dataset notation that appears next

A supervised dataset is a set of pairs

$$
\mathcal{D}=\bigl\{(x_i,y_i)\bigr\}_{i=1}^{n},
$$

said to be sampled **i.i.d.** from the unknown joint $P_{X,Y}$ (tilde notation $\sim$). What “i.i.d.” means is the next lecture.

---

## 7. Tiny concrete example

Suppose $2\times 2$ grayscale patches, so $D=4$. One observed patch might be

$$
x = (0.1,\ 0.8,\ 0.2,\ 0.7)\in\mathbb{R}^{4}.
$$

A binary label $y=1$ (“abnormal”) is **not** a fifth pixel of $x$; it is a value of a second RV $Y$ defined on the same experiment “patient imaged and labeled.” The object we want later is often $P(Y\mid X)$ — likelihood of the label given the image — which needs the joint world of $(X,Y)$.

---

## 8. Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|----------------|
| “The image *is* the random variable.” | Loosely said in class; precisely: the image is a **point in the range** of an RV. |
| Pixel values = probabilities | No — they are coordinates in $\mathbb{R}^{D}$. |
| Supervised vs unsupervised are totally different math | Both are distribution estimation; “label” is just another coordinate / RV. |
| Knowing one sample tells you $P_{X}$ | One point is not a distribution; we need many samples + structure (later lectures). |
